marker_malcolm.persona: Malcolm Ryan, COMP3180 unit convenor and marker, marking A2 Research Proposal fresh (round 8, independent), 19 Sep 2026, calibrated on this student's real A1 result (Content 65 / Presentation 55, marker comment: too much information per slide, no general overview, straight into technical detail).

criteria.descriptor_quote: At least five distinct and high-quality sources with a common theme relating to the project topic. Sources are very well summarised and evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness to the outlined project. Review synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships from the literature to motivate the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: The source base clears the HD count on paper: six counted peer-reviewed sources (Bertram et al. 2010, Ko et al. 2007, Pascarella et al. 2018, Dourish & Bellotti 1992, Whitson 2018, Maddila et al. 2023) plus Stray et al. 2016 and Washburn et al. 2016, all academic, all on one theme. The per-source work also clears my pet peeve cleanly - each entry names a specific mechanism or number and then says what it changes in the project ('Those 21 types give the think-alouds their coding frame'; 'That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it'). What stops it being 'expertly summarised and insightfully evaluated' is that the summaries are compressed past the point of being readable, and two of the eight are not evaluated at all. Three concrete reasons. (1) The orienting paragraph is six stacked one-sentence labels - 'Bertram et al. (2010) show where the record fails. Ko et al. (2007) give me a way to cut a producer's needs into pieces. Pascarella et al. (2018) show why games differ' - which is a list, not an overview; 'a way to cut a producer's needs into pieces' means nothing until four paragraphs later. This is the exact structure that cost this student marks at A1. (2) Individual sentences carry four loads at once: 'The taxonomy is a developer's, so only part of it transfers: "What have my coworkers been doing?" (Section 5.7) is a producer's question too, the debugging kinds are not, and Deliverable 1 tests the transfer by classifying the needs producers actually raise' is 46 words and three comma-spliced clauses; I had to read it twice, and so will anyone marking twenty of these. (3) The bounding paragraph gives Stray et al. (2016) and Washburn et al. (2016) one sentence each - 'Washburn et al. (2016) found no communication category among 155 game postmortems (pp. 280-289)' - which is a finding stated, not evaluated; the reader is never told what the categories were, so the inference 'postmortems record outcomes, not reporting' is asserted rather than earned. Two smaller accuracy worries: Dourish and Bellotti (1992) is characterised as 'watched four groups of three designers solve a 90-minute design problem in a shared editor', which foregrounds the empirical study over what that paper is actually known for; and 'Their own example is the version-control edit log, today's commit message' quietly attributes the student's own gloss to them. Neither is fatal, but both are the kind of thing I will push on.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Replace the six-label opening paragraph with three or four plain sentences that say, in ordinary words and with no citations, what question the literature is being asked and what the three answers on offer are ('Two explanations compete for why a team's record is thinner than its work: the reporting is structured against the reporter, or the tools hide what happened. A third, the audience, appears late. Two further studies describe what a game week and a reader's needs actually contain.'). Then split the three worst multi-clause sentences (the Ko transfer sentence, the 'The six do three jobs' sentence, and the Pascarella ownership sentence) into two each. Pay for the words by deleting the duplicated Dourish and Bellotti mechanism - it is stated in the opening paragraph and again in full at 'asking people to report costs the reporter and pays the group' - and by cutting the parenthetical '(owned means above a 75% contribution share)', which defines a term the paragraph does not otherwise use.

criteria.descriptor_quote: Outlines a sensible plan with clear and specific learning goals for developing industry-relevant skills. Identifies a considered research question with an appropriate and achievable mixed methodology for evaluation. Overview of scoping work undertaken provides a strongly convincing argument for the feasibility of the project. Includes a description of specific and measurable project deliverables clearly demonstrating these goals and satisfying unit requirements.
criteria.why_not_higher: Much of this is what I asked for in the Week 4 lecture and it is done properly. Four learning goals, spanning understand to create, phrased as capabilities not deliverables, each with a stated measure, and each measure falsifiable ('unaided, state each mechanism, its source and a breakdown it predicts'). Industry relevance is evidenced, not asserted (six of nine sampled employers asking for progress reporting). The research question is genuinely interesting and is decomposed into two sub-questions that each have a method attached. The methodology is truly mixed - scored comprehension items at Endsley's three levels on one arm, think-alouds coded against Ko's 21 types with a re-coding agreement check on the other - plus a fidelity check with a stated pass threshold before any participant sees anything, which is more methodological care than I usually see at A2. The scoping evidence is far past 'hello world': a working Unity 6.4 Editor package shown docked in the Editor (Figure 2), an exported report in Appendix C, a build-report probe for the stretch tier, a six-repository corpus measurement that motivates Figure 1, and a measured 46-100% naming-presence range that the 60% target is then set against. Deliverables are nine, each with a success measure; the hours sum to 65 with exactly 15 in prac (I checked both); and the tiers are the Kickstarter structure I endorsed, with an explicit overrun rule. Four things keep it out of HD. (1) The central novelty claim is overstated against the student's own appendix. The Introduction says 'None of the seven reads the Unity asset layer to tell a producer what changed', but Appendix A lists Unity Production Pipeline as reading 'Builds, assets, version control' for 'Producers, artists, QA', and Anchorpoint as reading the 'Git history of Unity, Unreal and Godot projects'. The claim is only true on the full conjunction, and the flat sentence invites exactly the question I would ask in a viva. HD wants a plan that 'talks to the state of the art' without leaving a hole like that. (2) The evaluation has an unacknowledged confound: each participant reads baseline on one week and treatment on another, so condition is entangled with week content. Counterbalancing 'by week and order' with eight participants gives four per cell and does not remove a difference in how legible the two weeks are. The document never names this, and the honest sentence it does contain - 'eight readers show direction and failure points, not significance' - covers sample size, not confounding. (3) Deliverable 1 asks 13 hours to cover four tools heuristically evaluated, 10 job ads, 25 reviews, two interviews and a 25-need specification. That is optimistic, and the heuristic evaluation is run by one person with no mention of the single-evaluator limitation that the student's own cited sources (Nielsen & Molich 1990) establish. Since the hour table is a commitment to explain variance at A3, an optimistic line here is a cost the student pays later. (4) 'A high level of creativity or originality' is the HD phrase, and the committed tier is a path classifier over a git-log export plus object-name extraction from YAML, with targets of 90% categorised and 60% named. It is well-argued and well-scoped, but as an artefact it is modest next to what a room of this cohort will submit, and the originality sits in the framing rather than the build. Two readability faults also sit inside this criterion because they obscure the plan: 'twice a week apart' reads as 'twice a week' on first pass, and 'an overrun consumes these two tiers first' has an ambiguous referent after three tiers have been named.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Fix the novelty claim and the confound, in two sentences. Replace 'None of the seven reads the Unity asset layer to tell a producer what changed; that is the gap this project fills' with 'Two read the asset layer but report to artists and QA (Anchorpoint, n.d.; Unity Technologies, n.d.), and the producer-facing ones read tickets or the repository only; none turns the asset layer into a week's account for a producer.' Then add one sentence to the study paragraph: 'Because each reader sees a different week in each condition, week difficulty is a rival explanation; I report the per-week baseline scores alongside the differences, and treat a week with a large baseline gap as uninterpretable.' Pay for both by cutting 'Deliverable 1 runs first and produces the needs list; its heuristic evaluation records what existing tools already answer', which repeats what the Deliverables table and the final schedule sentence both already say.

criteria.descriptor_quote: The report is easy to read and uses appropriate language and structure. It meets the word count, referencing and other submission requirements. It may contain a few minor spelling, grammatical or referencing errors.
criteria.why_not_higher: Everything mechanical is right. Structure follows the template, the three figures are relevant, numbered, captioned and cited at the point of use, Figure 1 is clean and legible and Figure 3 is genuinely well annotated, the body is 2,465 words against a 2,500 limit excluding references, the reference list is APA-consistent with DOIs and retrieval dates, every in-text citation appears in the list and every list entry is cited somewhere (McShaffry only in Appendix A, which is legitimate), and appendices hold non-vital material as they should. There is no spelling or grammatical error I can find. The Introduction is also a real improvement on this student's A1: its first three sentences are plain and give the reader an ordinary-language picture before any citation appears. But 'very easy to read' is not true of this document, and that is the D descriptor. From the Literature Review onward almost every sentence carries a citation, a number, a page reference and a use-claim simultaneously, with almost no low-density connective prose between them, and the Scoping Evidence section is a wall of specification with no orienting sentence at its head. This is the same register that drew 'So much information in each slide... You jumped straight into very technical details without providing context' from the A1 marker, and readability is weighted here, not in the other two criteria. Sentences I had to read twice, in order of appearance: 'Ko et al. (2007) give me a way to cut a producer's needs into pieces.'; 'The taxonomy is a developer's, so only part of it transfers...'; 'In games, sub-teams form around non-code categories such as multimedia (owned means above a 75% contribution share).'; 'Whitson's answer is therefore opacity: the tool hides causes...' (the 'therefore' does not follow from the two sentences before it); 'The six do three jobs: Bertram and Maddila show the record failing and the bar a fix must clear; Dourish and Bellotti and Whitson explain why...' ('Dourish and Bellotti and Whitson' stalls the eye); 'Each need in Deliverable 1's specification is marked derivable, partly derivable or not against a named artefact, twice a week apart, with disagreements reported.'; 'The prototype classifies files only; the committed tier adds object naming (Figure 3), where the AssetDatabase resolves identifiers to asset and script names without a parser.'; 'Across four SS3D weeks, 46-100% of changed prefabs and scenes carry an object name in their changed text (23 of 26 in the week shown).'; 'The target is eight readers, six of whom also think aloud, with a floor of five for each.'; 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough to test tracker fusion, and my own team's would not either: its sprint pages were backfilled for a semester and none of its 126 commits cites a Jira issue (Appendix A).' (44 words, and 'backfilled for a semester' is never explained); 'The challenge tier (2 hours) flags work gone quiet on two weeks and stays gated because Maddila et al. (2023) show ungated alerting misfires; an overrun consumes these two tiers first.' Deliverable 1's success-measure cell is also a 60-word run-on inside a table cell. Eleven sentences needing a second read in a 2,465-word document is the documented failure mode, not a stylistic quibble, and when torn between D and CR I report the lower band.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Do a single own-voice read-aloud pass with one rule: any sentence over 30 words or with more than two clauses gets split, and each of the three main sections gets one plain opening sentence that says what is coming before any number or citation appears. Two examples. At the head of Scoping Evidence, before the research question: 'The tool already runs; what follows is what it does today, what the committed version adds, and how eight readers will be tested on it.' For the 'twice a week apart' sentence: 'Deliverable 1's specification marks each need derivable, partly derivable or not derivable, against a named artefact. I repeat the marking a week later and report where the two passes disagree.' Pay for the added words by cutting 'Deliverable 1 runs first and produces the needs list; its heuristic evaluation records what existing tools already answer' and by trimming the duplicated Dourish and Bellotti gloss in the Literature Review's opening paragraph.

top_changes.location: Introduction, final paragraph: 'Seven surveyed tools each cover one part (Appendix A)...' ending 'None of the seven reads the Unity asset layer to tell a producer what changed; that is the gap this project fills.'
top_changes.problem: The central novelty claim is contradicted by the student's own Appendix A, which lists Unity Production Pipeline as reading 'Builds, assets, version control' for 'Producers, artists, QA' and Anchorpoint as reading the git history of Unity projects. The flat 'none of the seven' is only true on a conjunction the sentence does not state, and it is the first thing an informed marker will attack.
top_changes.fix: Replace the final sentence with: 'Two read the asset layer but report to artists and QA (Anchorpoint, n.d.; Unity Technologies, n.d.), and the producer-facing ones read tickets or the repository only; none turns the asset layer into a week's account for a producer.' Pay for the extra words by cutting 'Deliverable 1 runs first and produces the needs list; its heuristic evaluation records what existing tools already answer' from Scoping Evidence, which the Deliverables table and the closing schedule sentence both already say.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal: removes the single biggest viva-style hole in the state-of-the-art argument. Worth 2-3 marks on that criterion and it is the cheapest fix in the document.

top_changes.location: Literature Review, opening paragraph: 'Why is a team's shared record thinner than the work it describes? Two explanations compete. Dourish and Bellotti (1992) blame the structure of reporting...'
top_changes.problem: Six one-sentence source labels stacked as a roadmap. 'Ko et al. (2007) give me a way to cut a producer's needs into pieces' is meaningless until four paragraphs later. This is structurally the A1 failure - straight into detail with no plain overview - reproduced in prose.
top_changes.fix: Keep the opening question, then give three plain sentences naming the three explanations and the two descriptive studies without per-source labels: 'Two explanations compete: the reporting is structured against the reporter (Dourish & Bellotti, 1992), or the tools hide what happened (Whitson, 2018). A third, the audience, appears later (Stray et al., 2016). Two further studies describe what a game week and a reader's needs actually contain (Pascarella et al., 2018; Ko et al., 2007), and two show the record failing and the bar a fix must clear (Bertram et al., 2010; Maddila et al., 2023).' Pay for it by deleting the duplicated structural gloss at 'asking people to report costs the reporter and pays the group' in the Dourish and Bellotti paragraph.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review and Communication together: this is the change most likely to move Communication from CR to D, worth about 7 marks on that criterion and 1-2 on the review.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence, study paragraph: 'A pilot session runs first; its data is excluded. Each session then lasts 45 minutes. Eight student producers each read a baseline report for one team-week and a treatment report for another, counterbalanced by week and order.'
top_changes.problem: Condition is confounded with week content. Each reader sees baseline on one week and treatment on another, so a difference in how legible the two weeks are is a rival explanation for any treatment effect. The proposal never names this; the honest line about n=8 covers sample size, not confounding.
top_changes.fix: Add after the counterbalancing sentence: 'Because each reader sees a different week in each condition, week difficulty is a rival explanation; I report per-week baseline scores alongside the differences and treat a week with a large baseline gap as uninterpretable.' Pay for it by cutting 'Student producers and briefed proxies stand in for studio producers, a limit I report' down to 'Briefed proxies stand in for studio producers, a limit I report.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal: closes the methodological gap that most separates 'appropriate and achievable' from 'highly appropriate'. Worth 2-3 marks.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence, sub-question paragraph: 'Each need in Deliverable 1's specification is marked derivable, partly derivable or not against a named artefact, twice a week apart, with disagreements reported.'
top_changes.problem: 'Twice a week apart' parses first as 'twice a week'. This is a method description the marker must understand to credit Sub-question 1, and it is ambiguous.
top_changes.fix: Split into two sentences: 'Deliverable 1's specification marks each need derivable, partly derivable or not derivable, against a named artefact. I repeat the marking a week later and report where the two passes disagree.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication, and protects Project Proposal credit for Sub-question 1's method. About 1-2 marks on Communication.

top_changes.location: Deliverables, tier paragraph: 'The challenge tier (2 hours) flags work gone quiet on two weeks and stays gated because Maddila et al. (2023) show ungated alerting misfires; an overrun consumes these two tiers first.'
top_changes.problem: 'These two tiers' has an ambiguous referent after three tiers have been named in three consecutive sentences. Also, that the three tiers sum to Deliverable 2's 16 hours is left for the reader to compute.
top_changes.fix: End the paragraph: 'An overrun consumes the challenge tier first, then the stretch tier; the committed tier is not negotiable. The three tiers are Deliverable 2's 16 hours.' Pay for it by cutting 'which the prototype already reads (Appendix C)' from the stretch-tier sentence - Appendix C already carries the probe.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication and Project Proposal: makes the Kickstarter structure legible at a glance. About 1 mark each.

top_changes.location: Deliverables table, row 1 success measure: 'Four free-tier tools coded against Nielsen and Molich's (1990) and Nielsen's (1994) heuristics (5 h); 10 job ads and 25 reviews coded (3 h); two 20-minute interviews outside the reader pool (2 h); a spec classifying 25 needs...'
top_changes.problem: Two things at once. The cell is a 60-word run-on that is hard to read in a table, and the heuristic evaluation is run by one person with no mention of the single-evaluator limitation that the student's own cited source establishes - a marker who knows Nielsen and Molich will notice the omission in a project whose whole subject is tool usability.
top_changes.fix: Shorten the cell to semicolon-separated fragments without the inner parentheses where possible, and add one sentence to the Scoping Evidence or Deliverables prose: 'A single evaluator finds only a minority of a tool's usability problems (Nielsen & Molich, 1990), so Deliverable 1's heuristic pass is reported as a scoping instrument, not a usability verdict.' Pay for it by cutting 'Deliverable 1 runs across the break and Week 9' from the final schedule sentence and folding that week into the sentence that already places Deliverable 1 first.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal: turns an omission into visible evaluative thinking, which is what I said I look for. 1-2 marks.

top_changes.location: Literature Review, Ko paragraph: 'The taxonomy is a developer's, so only part of it transfers: "What have my coworkers been doing?" (Section 5.7) is a producer's question too, the debugging kinds are not, and Deliverable 1 tests the transfer by classifying the needs producers actually raise.'
top_changes.problem: 46 words, three comma-spliced clauses, and the load-bearing transfer argument buried in the middle of them. This is the single densest sentence in the document and it carries the justification for using a developer taxonomy on producers.
top_changes.fix: Split: 'The taxonomy is a developer's, so only part of it transfers. "What have my coworkers been doing?" (Section 5.7) is a producer's question too; the debugging kinds are not. Deliverable 1 tests that transfer by classifying the needs producers actually raise.' No net word cost.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication and Literature Review. Part of the CR-to-D case on Communication.

top_changes.location: Appendix B, item 5: 'Fixed answer: airlock interaction and sound, because 18 airlock prefab entries changed in two commits on one day; the treatment version names the nine prefabs.'
top_changes.problem: Unverified arithmetic. Appendix C shows the two airlock commits (#611 and #608) at 9 files each, 18 files total - but those 18 cannot all be prefab entries, since both commits will include .meta, code and art entries. As written, '18 airlock prefab entries' looks like a file count relabelled as a prefab count, and it is the fixed answer to a scored item.
top_changes.fix: Recount from the export and state the basis, for example '18 airlock entries (nine prefabs and their .meta files) changed in two commits on one day'. If the count does not hold, replace the number with the one that does.
top_changes.mark_impact: Not directly marked (appendix), but an unsupported number inside a scored instrument is the kind of thing that costs credibility on the Scoping Evidence argument. Fix it because it is cheap.

top_changes.location: Literature Review, synthesis paragraph: 'The six do three jobs: Bertram and Maddila show the record failing and the bar a fix must clear; Dourish and Bellotti and Whitson explain why; Pascarella and Ko describe what a game week and a reader's needs contain.'
top_changes.problem: 'Dourish and Bellotti and Whitson' stalls the reader on a repeated conjunction, in the one sentence that is doing the synthesis work the rubric explicitly rewards.
top_changes.fix: 'The six do three jobs. Bertram and Maddila show the record failing and the bar a fix must clear. Dourish and Bellotti, with Whitson, explain why. Pascarella and Ko describe what a game week and a reader's needs contain.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication, and protects the Literature Review's strongest paragraph. Under a mark, but free.

top_changes.location: Learning Goals, final paragraph: 'six of nine producer advertisements sampled in September 2026 ask for progress reporting to leadership or partners (Appendix A)'
top_changes.problem: Appendix A says six of the nine distinct employers, not six of nine advertisements - the sample was ten advertisements from nine employers. A small slip, but it is a number in the industry-relevance argument, and inconsistency between body and appendix is exactly what a careful marker checks.
top_changes.fix: 'six of the nine employers in a ten-advertisement sample taken in September 2026 ask for progress reporting to leadership or partners (Appendix A)'.
top_changes.mark_impact: Under a mark, but removes a body-versus-appendix mismatch.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the student has read the six counted sources in full, rather than working from verified extracts. The GenAI statement ends with an unresolved bracket on exactly this point.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: The student answering it for himself before submission, and being able to give an unaided potted summary of each of the six - the exercise I prescribed in the Week 4 lecture. If he cannot do that for a source, that source should be demoted out of the counted six rather than defended in the viva.

evidence_needed.item: The Appendix B item 5 count: whether 18 airlock prefab entries actually changed in commits #611 and #608, given Appendix C shows those commits at 9 files each in total.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Re-running the export filter on those two commits and reporting prefab entries separately from .meta, code and art entries.

evidence_needed.item: Whether Dourish and Bellotti (1992) actually reports four groups of three designers on a 90-minute task, as the review states, and whether 'their own example is the version-control edit log' is their example or the student's gloss.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A page citation for both claims from the published CSCW '92 paper. If the edit-log framing is the student's, say so explicitly - it costs nothing and it is honest.

evidence_needed.item: Recruitment. The study depends on eight student producers found at the Weeks 9 and 10 COMP3151 pracs, with a floor of five, and the whole evaluation design stands on it.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Named or counted commitments before Week 9 - even an informal list of who has said yes - and a stated fallback if fewer than five materialise beyond 'the quantitative arm is reported descriptively'.

evidence_needed.item: Whether Unity Production Pipeline, in closed beta with public availability stated as November 2026, will produce a producer-facing change report before the project's evaluation runs.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A dated recheck of Unity's public documentation in Week 9 or 10, recorded in the development diary. If it ships something close, the differentiation sentence needs rewriting rather than the project abandoning.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the 13 hours budgeted for Deliverable 1 is realistic for four heuristic evaluations, 10 job ads, 25 reviews, two interviews and a 25-need specification.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Timing the first tool's heuristic pass end to end and extrapolating, in Week 9, then adjusting the table before the tiers freeze in Week 11. Remember that the table is a commitment to explain variance at A3, so an honest number now is worth more than an optimistic one.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the two study weeks are comparably legible, which the confound in priority 3 turns on.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Generating both weeks' baseline reports before the pilot and checking that their commit counts, category spreads and total entries are in the same range; if they are not, reselect one week.

marker_malcolm.notes: SENTENCES THAT NEEDED A SECOND READ (density is this student's documented failure mode, so I list all of them): 1. 'Ko et al. (2007) give me a way to cut a producer's needs into pieces.' - metaphor with no referent at that point in the text. 2. 'The taxonomy is a developer's, so only part of it transfers: "What have my coworkers been doing?" (Section 5.7) is a producer's question too, the debugging kinds are not, and Deliverable 1 tests the transfer by classifying the needs producers actually raise.' - 46 words, three spliced clauses. 3. 'In games, sub-teams form around non-code categories such as multimedia (owned means above a 75% contribution share).' - the parenthetical defines 'owned', a word the sentence does not use. 4. 'Whitson's answer is therefore opacity: the tool hides causes, and blaming the tool rather than a teammate keeps the team moving.' - the 'therefore' does not follow from the shark-model sentence before it. 5. 'The six do three jobs: ... Dourish and Bellotti and Whitson explain why ...' - repeated conjunction. 6. 'Each need in Deliverable 1's specification is marked derivable, partly derivable or not against a named artefact, twice a week apart, with disagreements reported.' - 'twice a week apart' parses wrongly first. 7. 'The prototype classifies files only; the committed tier adds object naming (Figure 3), where the AssetDatabase resolves identifiers to asset and script names without a parser.' - 'without a parser' arrives with no set-up. 8. 'Across four SS3D weeks, 46-100% of changed prefabs and scenes carry an object name in their changed text (23 of 26 in the week shown).' - two different denominators in one sentence. 9. 'The target is eight readers, six of whom also think aloud, with a floor of five for each.' - 'each' refers to two different groups. 10. 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough to test tracker fusion, and my own team's would not either: its sprint pages were backfilled for a semester and none of its 126 commits cites a Jira issue (Appendix A).' - 44 words; 'backfilled for a semester' is never explained. 11. 'The challenge tier (2 hours) flags work gone quiet on two weeks and stays gated because Maddila et al. (2023) show ungated alerting misfires; an overrun consumes these two tiers first.' - ambiguous 'these two tiers'. 12. Deliverables table row 1's success-measure cell - a 60-word run-on inside a table cell. Eleven-plus second-read sentences in 2,465 words is why Communication sits at CR rather than D, and it is the same fault the A1 marker named.  CONTRADICTIONS AND UNSUPPORTED NUMBERS: (a) Introduction's 'None of the seven reads the Unity asset layer to tell a producer what changed' versus Appendix A's rows for Unity Production Pipeline ('Builds, assets, version control'; 'Producers, artists, QA') and Anchorpoint ('Git history of Unity, Unreal and Godot projects') - the sharpest attack surface in the document, priority 1. (b) Appendix B item 5's '18 airlock prefab entries' against Appendix C's #611 at 9 files and #608 at 9 files - 18 total files, which cannot all be prefab entries; priority 8. (c) Body's 'six of nine producer advertisements' versus Appendix A's 'six of the nine employers' from a ten-advertisement sample; priority 10. (d) Appendix A sets a screening threshold of 30 genuine issue references per 100 commits and reports that the best repository reached 20, so nothing met the threshold; the body then says the Unity Experiment Framework, 'the best-linked, serves Sub-question 1'. That is defensible but requires the reader to reconcile a threshold that nothing passed with a repository still being used - one clause would fix it. (e) The three tiers (11 + 3 + 2 hours) do reconcile with Deliverable 2's 16 hours, but the document never says so.  MECHANICAL-TRAP CHECK: Template instruction text - none present in the body. Cover fields - title, subtitle, name and header present; Topic Category present and filled ('Developer / production tools'); Student ID is the known '[STUDENT ID]' placeholder, and the GenAI statement ends with the known bracketed CONFIRM line. Both are on the student's own pre-submission list and I have marked the document as if they were filled, but they must not survive to submission - a placeholder on the cover page reads as carelessness on a criterion that explicitly covers submission requirements. Word count - 2,465 body plus 27 cover, under the 2,500 limit excluding the reference list; only the overall limit is enforced, and it is met. Hours - table sums to 65 (13+16+4+3+14+7+4+2+2) with in-prac column summing to 15 (2+5+1+1+4+1+1+0+0); both correct, and the 50-outside/15-in-prac split is stated. Figures - three, numbered, captioned, each cited at the point of use (Figure 1 in the Pascarella paragraph, Figures 2 and 3 in Scoping Evidence and Figure 3 again in the tier paragraph); all three are relevant rather than decorative, Figure 1 is clean and legible, Figure 3 is well annotated, Figure 2's Editor screenshot has small text but is legible at page width and Figure 2's caption is consistent with Appendix C's date range. GenAI statement - present, dated July to September 2026, names the tool, itemises five AI-introduced errors caught and corrected, and points to GENAI-EVIDENCE.md; this is the right way to declare it and the error list is a strength, not a liability. References - APA-consistent with DOIs and retrieval dates; I checked both directions and found no orphan either way (McShaffry 2013 is cited only in Appendix A, which is acceptable). Appendices - correctly used for non-vital material; nothing load-bearing is hidden there, which matters because I do not promise to read them.  OVERALL: predicted 78 (0.45x79 + 0.40x79 + 0.15x73 = 78.1). This is a genuinely strong D that is held out of HD by three things, in order: the density that already cost this student twenty-odd marks at A1, the novelty claim that its own appendix undercuts, and a confound in the study design that goes unnamed. None of the three is expensive to fix, and priorities 1 to 3 alone are worth roughly five marks. I would also note a realistic floor: if a marker reads this quickly and the density bites across all three criteria rather than only Communication, it lands nearer 72.

marker_mitchell.persona: Mitchell McEwan, COMP3180 lecturer (usability research; Week 5 source-quality/CARS lecture; Monday prac convenor). Round 8, marked fresh and strict, reporting the lower band when torn, and calibrated against this student's A1 outcome (AI predicted 88/82, real marker returned 65/55 with the comment that the work was too dense and gave no plain overview).

criteria.descriptor_quote: At least five distinct and high-quality sources with a common theme relating to the project topic. Sources are very well summarised and evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness to the outlined project. Review synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships from the literature to motivate the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: The HD band needs sources 'expertly summarised and insightfully evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness'. Evaluation here is uneven across the six. Four entries evaluate well: Pascarella gets a named sampling limitation ('No Unity or Unreal project appears in its sample'), Dourish and Bellotti get an explicit evidence critique ('Their evidence is narrow: four groups, one session'), Maddila gets three bounded limits, and Bertram gets a path-not-taken ('That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it'). But the Whitson entry is the thinnest in the review and contains no evaluation at all: 'Whitson (2018) describes 10 weeks of fieldwork with 10 intern developers at a large international game studio in Canada' is followed by two illustrations and a use, and never asks what ten interns at one studio can support, or what it means that the venue is a media-studies journal rather than an SE one. Across the whole review not one source is assessed for currency or bias, which are two of my four CARS headings: a 1992 CSCW study and a 2007 study of collocated teams are both load-bearing and neither is defended as still applicable. Second block: the review's opening paragraph is not an overview, it is six consecutive source announcements ('Bertram et al. (2010) show where the record fails. Ko et al. (2007) give me a way to cut a producer's needs into pieces.'), so the reader meets six names and three mechanisms before being told what the section is going to argue. That is the same missing-overview problem the A1 marker named, and it costs the 'expertly synthesises' half of the HD descriptor even though the closing synthesis paragraph itself is genuinely strong. I am charging the general prose density to Communication rather than here, but the density inside the source entries (nearly every sentence carries a number, a section reference or a page number) is why I will not call these summaries expert.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Replace the six-announcement opening paragraph with a two-sentence overview that names the question and the three competing explanations, and spend the words freed on a quality-and-limits clause for Whitson (ten interns, one studio, an ethnographic account rather than a measured one) plus one clause somewhere defending why a 1992 and a 2007 study still hold for a 2026 Unity team. That converts six well-used sources into six evaluated sources and gives the marker the roadmap before the detail.

criteria.descriptor_quote: Outlines a sensible plan with clear and specific learning goals for developing industry-relevant skills. Identifies a considered research question with an appropriate and achievable mixed methodology for evaluation. Overview of scoping work undertaken provides a strongly convincing argument for the feasibility of the project. Includes a description of specific and measurable project deliverables clearly demonstrating these goals and satisfying unit requirements.
criteria.why_not_higher: Two things hold this off HD, and the first is structural rather than cosmetic. (1) The headline research question is 'Which of a producer's information needs can be answered automatically from the artefacts a team already produces - and which can't?', and its method is Sub-question 1: 'Each need in Deliverable 1's specification is marked derivable, partly derivable or not against a named artefact, twice a week apart, with disagreements reported.' That is the researcher classifying his own list against his own artefacts and then checking his own consistency a week later. Intra-rater agreement on one's own judgement is the weakest evidence in the proposal, and it is carrying the primary question. The eight participants only serve Sub-question 2 (does naming scenes and prefabs improve comprehension). So the mixed methodology is real - quantitative comprehension scoring at Endsley's three levels plus a coded think-aloud - but it is pointed at the secondary question, and HD wants a 'highly appropriate' methodology for the question actually asked. (2) Achievability of the participant arm, which is where student projects fail. 'The target is eight readers, six of whom also think aloud, with a floor of five for each', 'A pilot session runs first; its data is excluded', 'Each session then lasts 45 minutes', and the calendar puts 'sessions in Week 12'. That is nine 45-minute sessions inside one week, against Deliverable 5's budget of '7' hours for 'Eight 45-minute sessions plus scheduling and setup' - the session clock alone is six hours, leaving under an hour for the pilot, scheduling, no-shows and setup, and the pilot is not in the count at all. Recruiting 'at the Weeks 9 and 10 COMP3151 pracs' for Week 12 sessions leaves a two-to-three week attrition gap with no re-contact plan. Everything else is at or above HD: four Bloom-spread learning goals each with a stated Measure, a working Unity 6.4 Editor package screenshotted on real repository data (Figure 2), a six-repository corpus measurement including his own team's, a measured 46-100% naming range, a build-report probe, a fidelity check with a pass threshold and a repair week, explicit out-of-scope statements, and committed/stretch/challenge tiers whose 11+3+2 hours reconcile exactly with Deliverable 2's 16. The scoping is well past 'hello world' and I would call it advanced. But torn between bands I report the lower, and the feasibility arithmetic plus the self-answered primary question put it at the top of D rather than into HD.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Give Sub-question 1 a participant-grounded check and fix the session arithmetic in the same edit: state that the two Deliverable 1 interviewees and the six think-aloud follow-ups independently mark a sample of the needs list, and that agreement with my classification is reported (this turns a self-consistency check into a small inter-rater result); then move the pilot and three sessions into Week 11 and raise Deliverable 5 from 14 to 16 hours, paying for it from Deliverable 1's three-hour job-ad-and-review coding.

criteria.descriptor_quote: The report is easy to read and uses appropriate language and structure. It meets the word count, referencing and other submission requirements. It may contain a few minor spelling, grammatical or referencing errors.
criteria.why_not_higher: The D band requires the report to be 'very easy to read'. It is not. It is compressed to the point of being effortful, and I had to re-read eleven sentences (listed in notes) to extract their meaning. Concretely: (a) a central corpus is never introduced - 'Across four SS3D weeks, 46-100% of changed prefabs and scenes carry an object name in their changed text' is the first appearance of SS3D in the document and it is never expanded or described, so a marker who does not read Appendix A does not know it is an open-source Unity game, yet both study weeks come from it; (b) 'the committed tier adds object naming (Figure 3)' in Scoping Evidence uses a term that is not defined until the Deliverables section two pages later, and the same for 'stretch' and 'challenge'; (c) 'Across four SS3D weeks, 46-100% ... (23 of 26 in the week shown). The 60% naming target is set against that range' asks the reader to hold three numbers and infer the link between a 46-100% range and a 60% target; (d) 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough to test tracker fusion, and my own team's would not either: its sprint pages were backfilled for a semester and none of its 126 commits cites a Jira issue (Appendix A). The study reads the asset layer only; both report weeks come from SS3D, and the Unity Experiment Framework, the best-linked, serves Sub-question 1.' - two sentences carrying a screening result, a negative finding about his own team, a scope cut and a corpus split, with 'the best-linked' dropped in as a bare appositive; (e) the register slips once, 'Ko et al. (2007) give me a way to cut a producer's needs into pieces', which is colloquial against an otherwise clinical document; (f) the sentence 'The taxonomy is a developer's, so only part of it transfers: "What have my coworkers been doing?" (§5.7) is a producer's question too, the debugging kinds are not, and Deliverable 1 tests the transfer by classifying the needs producers actually raise' runs three independent clauses off one colon with a comma splice in the middle. Against that: the word count is met (2,465 body), all three figures are numbered, captioned and cited in the body and all three genuinely earn their place, the reference list is APA-consistent and I found no citation missing from it or entry missing a citation, no template instruction text survives, the GenAI statement is specific and creditable, and I found no spelling errors. The Introduction does open plainly ('Each week a game producer needs to know what changed'), which is a real improvement on the A1 pattern - but it is the only place in the document that orients the reader, and it is spent in five sentences. Given how hard the A1 marker punished density and a missing overview on this same project, I will not credit this as 'very easy to read'.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Buy roughly 60 words by deleting the four one-line source announcements in the Literature Review's opening paragraph, and spend them on orientation: one sentence introducing SS3D and the corpus at the top of Scoping Evidence ('The study uses SS3D, a large open-source Unity game with six years of history, as its source of real team-weeks'), one clause glossing the three tiers at their first mention, and splitting the two longest sentences in (d) and (f) above into four. Nothing needs to be added that is not already implied - the document needs air, not content.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence: "ChangeLens is a Unity Editor package (Unity 6.4): it reads a git log export for one week..." and "Across four SS3D weeks, 46-100% of changed prefabs and scenes..."
top_changes.problem: SS3D is the backbone of the whole evaluation - both report weeks, the naming measurement, Figures 1, 2 and 3, and Appendix B all come from it - and it is never introduced. It appears first as a bare acronym in a percentage claim. A marker who does not open Appendix A has no idea what it is, which makes the scoping evidence read as unanchored. Same problem, smaller, for 'the committed tier', used before it is defined.
top_changes.fix: Insert at the head of the Scoping Evidence paragraph: 'The study's material is SS3D (Space Station 3D), a large open-source Unity game whose public history supplies real team-weeks.' Gloss the tier at first use: 'the committed tier (the version I commit to delivering) adds object naming'. Pay for it by cutting 'and where no name resolves the report falls back to the file path' (14 words, a detail that belongs in the repo README) and 'One item per report is unanswerable, to catch guessing' can be compressed to 'one item per report is unanswerable'.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication: this is the single change most likely to move CR to D, worth about 8 marks on that criterion (1.2 on the task). Also removes the most obvious Q&A hole.

top_changes.location: Literature Review, opening paragraph: "Why is a team's shared record thinner than the work it describes? Two explanations compete. ... Bertram et al. (2010) show where the record fails. Ko et al. (2007) give me a way to cut a producer's needs into pieces. Pascarella et al. (2018) show why games differ..."
top_changes.problem: The paragraph is six source announcements in a row. It is a list, not an overview, and it front-loads six author names before the reader knows what the review will argue. This is exactly the structure the A1 marker called out ('You jumped straight into very technical details without providing context'). It also drops the register once ('cut a producer's needs into pieces').
top_changes.fix: Keep the opening question and the two competing mechanisms, then replace the four remaining announcement sentences with one: 'Four further studies supply what those two explanations leave out: where the record fails, what a reader's needs contain, why a game week differs from a software week, and what a working absence-detector must avoid.' That is roughly 45 words saved.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review and Communication together; roughly 2 marks on LR (the 'expertly synthesises' half) and it funds priorities 1 and 3 from the word budget.

top_changes.location: Literature Review: "Whitson (2018) describes 10 weeks of fieldwork with 10 intern developers at a large international game studio in Canada."
top_changes.problem: This is the only one of the six counted sources with no evaluation of its quality or limits. Every other entry either names a sampling limitation, an evidence critique or a path not taken. Whitson carries one of the two competing mechanisms the whole project is built to adjudicate, and the entry does not say what ten interns at one studio can and cannot support, or note that it is an ethnographic account in a media-studies venue rather than a measured SE result. Against my CARS framing it is the weakest entry in an otherwise strong review, and it is the one I would ask about in the prac.
top_changes.fix: Add, using words freed by priority 2: 'Ten interns at one studio is a narrow base, and the account is interpretive rather than measured, so I take opacity as a hypothesis to test in the think-aloud rather than as an established rate.' Also soften the unexplained 'Whitson's answer is therefore opacity' to 'Whitson reads this as opacity'.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review, 2-3 marks; it is the difference between five evaluated sources and six.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence: "Sub-question 1: which surfaced needs can be derived, fully or partly, from the tracker export, the repository history and the Unity asset layer? Each need in Deliverable 1's specification is marked derivable, partly derivable or not against a named artefact, twice a week apart, with disagreements reported."
top_changes.problem: The primary research question is answered almost entirely by the researcher's own classification, checked only against himself a week later. That is intra-rater consistency, not evidence, and it means the human participants are only serving the secondary question. This is the strongest single reason the Project Proposal sits in D rather than HD, and it is also the thing I would push hardest on in a 1-on-1.
top_changes.fix: Extend the sentence: '...twice a week apart; the two Deliverable 1 interviewees and the six think-aloud participants each independently classify a ten-need sample, and agreement with my classification is reported alongside the disagreements.' Pay for the 25 words by cutting 'A pilot session runs first; its data is excluded' down to a clause inside the next sentence, and by cutting 'Deliverable 1 runs first and produces the needs list; its heuristic evaluation records what existing tools already answer', which duplicates the Deliverables table.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal, 4-6 marks; this is the credible route from 80 to the HD boundary on that criterion.

top_changes.location: Deliverables table row 5: "Eight 45-minute sessions plus scheduling and setup (7 h)" and the calendar sentence "...sessions in Week 12."
top_changes.problem: Eight 45-minute sessions is six hours of contact time before any scheduling, room booking, setup, no-shows or the pilot, which the proposal says runs first and is not costed anywhere. Nine sessions compressed into Week 12, with recruitment done in Weeks 9-10, is the classic point at which a student study collapses. The hour table is also a commitment you will have to explain at A3, so an optimistic number here costs twice.
top_changes.fix: Change the row to 'Ten 45-minute sessions including a pilot, plus scheduling, setup and one re-run slot (9 h); six think-alouds coded from timestamped notes (7 h)' and set Hours to 16, and change the calendar to 'the pilot and first sessions in Week 11, the remainder in Week 12'. Pay for the two hours by dropping Deliverable 1's '10 job ads and 25 reviews coded (3 h)' to '10 job ads and 15 reviews coded (2 h)' and the spec row from 3 h to 2 h, keeping the total at 65 and in-prac at 15.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal feasibility, 2-3 marks now, and it protects the A3 reflection where unexplained hour variance is explicitly marked down.

top_changes.location: Recruitment paragraph: "I recruit at the Weeks 9 and 10 COMP3151 pracs and my COMP3180 prac; every COMP3151 team has a student producer..."
top_changes.problem: Recruitment is where these projects die and the proposal states a plan, not a commitment. 'Every COMP3151 team has a student producer' is an argument that the pool exists, not that eight of them have agreed. There is a contingency for under-recruitment ('If fewer are recruited, the think-alouds run first') which is good, but no date by which the shortfall is detected.
top_changes.fix: Add one sentence: 'Slots are booked by the end of Week 10; if fewer than five readers are confirmed by then, I extend recruitment to the COMP3180 cohort and drop to the think-aloud-first design.' Pay with the redundant 'Participation in interviews and sessions is voluntary, with verbal consent and de-identified reporting' shortened to 'Participation is voluntary, with verbal consent and de-identified reporting.'
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal, 1-2 marks on the feasibility clause of the descriptor.

top_changes.location: Figure 1 caption: "Code share of changed-file entries in six Unity repositories, five open-source and my own team's: code is a minority in every one (7-36%)."
top_changes.problem: The claim 'code is a minority in every one' holds only on the basis charted, with .meta counted as non-code. Appendix A honestly reports the second basis, on which VRTK is 57% - code is a majority there. The caption states the strong version without the qualifier that the axis label carries, so a marker who reads Appendix A will see the body claim as slightly over-reaching and a marker who does not will be given an unqualified claim. The whole Pascarella argument leans on this figure.
top_changes.fix: Change the caption to '...my own team's: counting Unity .meta files as non-code, code is a minority in every one (7-36%); excluding .meta from both sides it remains a minority in four of six (Appendix A).' Costs about 18 words; pay from the Introduction sentence 'A two-day refactor can leave no ticket, while a three-line tweak can look like a day's work', which repeats the point the preceding sentence already made.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review credibility, about 1 mark, and it removes the easiest challenge I could put to you in the prac.

top_changes.location: Cover block: "%ID: [STUDENT ID]" and after the GenAI statement: "[CONFIRM BEFORE SUBMISSION: which of the six counted sources Raphael has read in full]"
top_changes.problem: Two unfilled placeholders. The student ID is a submission requirement the Communication criterion names explicitly. The CONFIRM line is an internal note that must not appear in a submitted document under any circumstances - it reads as an admission that the sources may not have been read, which is the worst possible thing to leave in a literature review.
top_changes.fix: Fill the ID. Delete the CONFIRM line entirely. Separately, before Monday, write a hundred-word summary of each of the six counted sources without looking at them - if you cannot, read the paper, because I will ask.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication; leaving either in costs 3-5 marks on that criterion and the CONFIRM line would invite a source-comprehension challenge in the 1-on-1.

top_changes.location: Figure 2: "ChangeLens docked in the Unity 6.4 Editor on the SS3D week of 8-14 February 2021 (commits on 10-14 February)."
top_changes.problem: The screenshot is a full Editor capture in the dark theme placed at 13 cm wide. The Summary and Changes-by-category panels - the only parts that evidence anything - occupy the middle third, while the top chrome and the truncated commit list at the bottom eat the width. top_changes.location: References: "Anchorpoint. (n.d.)...", "McShaffry, M. (2013, March)...", "Unity Technologies. (n.d.). Unity Production Pipeline..."
top_changes.problem: These three references are cited only inside Appendix A. Malcolm has said on the record that appendices may not be read. If they are not, three of the nineteen references look uncited, which reads as padding - the opposite of the impression you want on a criterion that rewards referencing discipline.

evidence_needed.item: Whether Raphael has read the six counted sources in full, rather than working from summaries. The CONFIRM placeholder in the document says this is unresolved, and the GenAI statement discloses heavy AI involvement in 'literature search and citation checking'.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A hundred-word unaided summary of each of the six, written without the papers open, naming the method, the sample and the one finding he uses. If he can do that for Bertram, Ko, Pascarella, Dourish and Bellotti, Whitson and Maddila, the review is his. I will ask for two of them at the Monday 1-on-1.

evidence_needed.item: Actual participant commitments. The proposal says 'I recruit at the Weeks 9 and 10 COMP3151 pracs' and targets eight readers with a floor of five, but no one has agreed yet.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A named list of COMP3151 teams and their producers with at least five provisional yes responses and booked slots by the end of Week 10, or the fallback design activated on a stated date.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the committed tier's object naming actually works. Figure 3 shows that names exist in the serialised text; it does not show ChangeLens resolving them. The 60% naming target rests on a measurement of what is present, not on what the tool produces.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the second study week can meet the same naming and fidelity thresholds. Only the 8-14 February 2021 SS3D week is measured in detail (23 of 26); the counterbalanced design needs two comparable weeks.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: The same naming-presence and category counts computed for the chosen second week, plus a statement of which week it is.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the fidelity check is costed realistically. Three hours to score every claim in two weeks' reports by hand against the team's record, with one hour reserved for repair, looks thin for a by-hand method.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A timed dry run of the fidelity scoring on the 8-14 February report - how many claims, how long per claim - reported in the development diary.

evidence_needed.item: Engagement evidence for the weekly 1-on-1. Attendance is now the primary engagement record for A3, and this student missed the Week 4 prac.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Regular attendance at the Monday prac from Week 9 onward with the working build shown, plus a dated diary entry each week as Deliverable 8 promises.

evidence_needed.item: Whether verbal consent and de-identified reporting is sufficient for this study design, given it involves recording think-alouds of classmates.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A short confirmation from Malcolm or me that the design sits inside the general student clearance, recorded in the diary - it almost certainly does, but the confirmation is free and worth having before Week 12.

marker_mitchell.notes:
SOURCE-BY-SOURCE CARS VERDICTS. Bertram et al. (2010), CSCW: PASSES CARS. Credibility - peer-reviewed CSCW, Greenberg and Walker are established CSCW and SE researchers. Accuracy - method and sample stated (interviews and survey, 15 people, four small collocated teams), quote given with participant code and page number (P05, p. 296), Team B located with a page reference. Reasonableness - no overclaim. Support - the entry attributes its numbers. Entry states what was specifically learnt ('Bugs go unfiled because the record fails at the point of entry') and how it is used, and adds a path not taken ('That remedy still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it'), which is the evaluative move I reward. Missing: no comment on what four small teams can support or on currency. Ko et al. (2007), ICSE: PASSES CARS. Top-tier venue, method and both samples given (17 observed, 42 surveyed), the finding is specific rather than titular (21 information types across seven kinds of work; 'What code caused this program state?' unsatisfied in 61% of cases, p. 351) and the reason is named (the obstacle was the tool, not a colleague). Usefulness is concrete and dual - unit of analysis plus the think-aloud coding frame - and the transfer limit is explicitly bounded. Strongest entry in the review alongside Pascarella. Missing: currency (collocated teams, 2007) unaddressed. Pascarella et al. (2018), MSR: PASSES CARS. Peer-reviewed, sample stated (30 game and 30 non-game repositories), the specific learning is the 80% versus 30% Development-category contrast plus ownership forming around non-code categories at a stated threshold (75% contribution share). The sampling limitation is named and then acted on - 'No public Unity or Unreal project appears in its sample, so I measured six Unity repositories myself' - which is the best single move in the document and is evidenced by Figure 1. Caveat under Support: the figure's 'minority in every one' claim holds only on the .meta-as-non-code basis (see change 7). Dourish and Bellotti (1992), CSCW: PASSES CARS with the currency question open. Foundational and correctly used; the specific learning is the structural mechanism (reporting costs the reporter and pays the group; recipients get what the sender judges relevant, when the sender chooses) and it is instantiated in his own corpus ('Fix restart bug (#588)' naming an intention while touching 35 files). Explicit evidence critique present: 'Their evidence is narrow: four groups, one session.' That is exactly the evaluation I want. Not addressed: why a 1992 finding about a shared editor transfers to a 2026 distributed Unity team. Whitson (2018), New Media and Society: PASSES CARS on credibility but the ENTRY DOES NOT EVALUATE IT. Peer-reviewed, author is an established games-production scholar, fieldwork base stated (10 weeks, 10 intern developers, a large international game studio in Canada - correctly not naming a city). The specific learning is present (the 'voodoo' framing, the shark model that would not animate) and the use is clear (the think-aloud follow-up asks what the page leaves unexplained). But there is no assessment of the evidence base, the venue, or the interpretive method, and this source carries one of the two competing mechanisms. Weakest of the six; see change 3. Maddila et al. (2023), TOSEM: PASSES CARS. Journal, Microsoft-scale deployment, and the entry is explicitly about what he learnt methodologically rather than what the paper is about ('what I learnt is how it avoids false alarms'), with a concrete number (86 of 119 rejected alerts had fired despite recent activity) and three named limits that bound his own claim. The use is a design constraint, not a citation of convenience: 'it must compose across items and read asset activity, or it adds nothing.' Excellent. Stray et al. (2016), JSS, synthesis only: peer-reviewed journal, 12 teams, and the specific learning is real (audience - a stand-up that becomes status reporting to the manager stops serving the team) and adds a third mechanism. Compressed to one sentence with no evaluation, but it is not one of the counted six. Washburn et al. (2016), ICSE Companion, synthesis only: correctly attributed, 155 postmortems, pp. 280-289 given, and it is used as a negative finding ('found no communication category'), which is legitimate evaluative use. Also uncounted. NET: six distinct, high-quality, peer-reviewed counted sources including academic research articles, so the HD source-count bar is met; what is not met is evaluation of all six on quality.

SENTENCES I HAD TO READ TWICE. 1. 'The taxonomy is a developer's, so only part of it transfers: "What have my coworkers been doing?" (§5.7) is a producer's question too, the debugging kinds are not, and Deliverable 1 tests the transfer by classifying the needs producers actually raise.' 2. 'Across four SS3D weeks, 46-100% of changed prefabs and scenes carry an object name in their changed text (23 of 26 in the week shown). The 60% naming target is set against that range, and where no name resolves the report falls back to the file path.' 3. 'ChangeLens is a Unity Editor package (Unity 6.4): it reads a git log export for one week, classifies each changed path by extension and sibling .meta file, and shows counts per category (Figure 2; Appendix C).' 4. 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough to test tracker fusion, and my own team's would not either: its sprint pages were backfilled for a semester and none of its 126 commits cites a Jira issue (Appendix A).' 5. 'The study reads the asset layer only; both report weeks come from SS3D, and the Unity Experiment Framework, the best-linked, serves Sub-question 1.' 6. 'Each need in Deliverable 1's specification is marked derivable, partly derivable or not against a named artefact, twice a week apart, with disagreements reported.' 7. 'The quantitative arm scores the six items against fixed answers at Endsley's (1995) three levels of situation awareness: what changed, what it means, what happens next.' 8. 'I report each participant's treatment-minus-baseline difference over five scored items, by item and level; eight readers show direction and failure points, not significance.' 9. 'The challenge tier (2 hours) flags work gone quiet on two weeks and stays gated because Maddila et al. (2023) show ungated alerting misfires; an overrun consumes these two tiers first.' 10. 'Measure: given an unfamiliar Unity week, I can tie each layout decision in its one-page report to a named reader need, two of them defended against a rejected alternative.' 11. 'Their own example is the version-control edit log, today's commit message; in my corpus, "Fix restart bug (#588)" names an intention while touching 35 files across five categories.' Eleven second-reads in a 2,465-word document is the density problem stated as a number, and it is the reason Communication is CR.

MECHANICAL-TRAP CHECK. Word count: body 2,465 plus 27 cover, under the 2,500 excluding references - PASS. Template instruction text: none survives - PASS. Cover fields: title, subtitle, name, Topic Category ('Developer / production tools') and running header all present; %ID is the placeholder [STUDENT ID] - FAIL until filled, noted once as instructed and marked as if filled. The bracketed CONFIRM line after the GenAI statement is the second placeholder, same treatment, but it must be deleted rather than filled. Hours: column sums to 65 (13+16+4+3+14+7+4+2+2) and in-prac to 15 (2+5+1+1+4+1+1+0+0) - PASS, and the stated split '50 outside class, 15 in prac' is consistent. Tier hours reconcile: committed 11 plus stretch 3 plus challenge 2 equals Deliverable 2's 16 - PASS, though the reader must do that arithmetic unaided. Figures: three, numbered 1-3, each captioned and each cited in the body text - PASS; Figure 2's legibility at 13 cm is marginal (change 9). Internal arithmetic checked: Appendix C categories sum to 104 (25+35+8+2+4+30) - PASS; Appendix B item 3's '45' equals 35+8+2 - PASS; Appendix A's five public repositories plus his own equals Figure 1's six bars - PASS; 'Seven surveyed tools' matches Appendix A's seven rows - PASS. GenAI statement: present, dated, names the tool and vendor, itemises what it touched, and discloses five corrected AI errors with evidence in an accompanying file - PASS, and this is a genuine strength rather than a compliance tick. References: 19 entries, APA-consistent, DOIs present where they exist and retrieval dates on the n.d. web sources; every in-text citation resolves to an entry and every entry is cited somewhere - PASS, with the caveat that McShaffry (2013), Anchorpoint (n.d.) and Unity Technologies (n.d.) appear only inside Appendix A (change 10). Endsley (1995) is cited as Human Factors 37(1), 32-64, which is the correct article for 'Toward a theory of situation awareness' rather than the companion measurement paper - correct. Spelling and grammar: no spelling errors found; one comma splice inside the Ko entry, and Washburn's 'Jr.' placement in the reference is slightly unusual but defensible.

CONTRADICTIONS AND TENSIONS. (a) Figure 1's caption claim 'code is a minority in every one' versus Appendix A's second basis, on which VRTK is 57% code - honestly disclosed in the appendix but not qualified in the caption. (b) The Introduction frames the project as fusing tracker and repository signals ('reads the files a team already produces'), and the gap statement in the same paragraph is that no tool 'reads the Unity asset layer to tell a producer what changed' - but Scoping Evidence then rules tracker fusion out entirely ('A live tracker connection is out of scope'). The two are reconcilable and the reason is given, but the Introduction's framing is broader than what is actually being built, and a marker reading the Introduction then the Deliverables will notice the narrowing. Worth one clause in the Introduction acknowledging the scope. (c) Deliverable 5 budgets eight sessions while the method describes nine including the uncosted pilot. (d) 'The target is eight readers, six of whom also think aloud, with a floor of five for each' means the floor for think-alouds equals five of a floor of five readers, which is arithmetically tight but not wrong - it just needed a second read.

OVERALL AND HONEST RANGE. 0.45x79 + 0.40x80 + 0.15x72 = 35.55 + 32.00 + 10.80 = 78.35, rounded to 78. That is the upper end of my honest range. This is a substantively strong proposal - six properly used peer-reviewed sources, a genuinely mixed methodology, a working prototype on real data, and an hour table that actually adds up - and if I marked only the substance it would sit at the D/HD boundary. But the A1 calibration on this same project is a warning I have to take seriously: the real marker returned 65 and 55 against AI predictions of 88 and 82, and the comment named density and a missing overview, both of which are still present here in the Literature Review's opening and throughout Scoping Evidence. A marker who reacts to this document the way the A1 marker reacted to the deck could land Literature Review at 70 and Communication at 62-65, which gives a task mark near 72. I would not predict below that, because the Introduction does now open plainly and the learning goals - which the A1 marker singled out as good - are better here than they were there. Predicted 78; realistic floor 72.
